title: Configuration
description: Configure Herdr keybindings, themes, sidebar behavior, notifications, and advanced options.
---

See [Monitoring, account usage and docking](/docs/monitoring/) for host metrics, provider account bindings, and movable terminal groups.


Herdr works without a config file. Add one when you want custom keys, themes, sidebar layouts, notifications, or advanced behavior.

The [Config reference](/docs/config-reference/) lists every setting and keybinding, with types, defaults, and allowed values. This page covers setup, common recipes, and configuration structures that need more explanation than a reference row.

## Before you connect

You need normal SSH access to the remote machine. Verify it first:

```bash
ssh workbox
```

`workbox` can be a host from your SSH config. You can also use a target such as `ssh://you@server:2222`.

Multi-machine connections are supported on Linux and macOS clients, connecting to Linux and macOS servers on x86_64 or aarch64. Multi-machine connections are not yet verified or supported on Windows; standalone `herdr --remote` remains supported on Windows. Native Windows servers are not supported as SSH targets. See [Remote attach over SSH](/docs/persistence-remote/#remote-attach-over-ssh) for SSH configuration, authentication, and custom binaries.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Add a machine
chunks.text:
## Add a machine

Run setup in an interactive terminal so Herdr can ask before installing or replacing anything:

```bash
herdr machine add workbox --label "Build machine"
```

This uses the remote default session. A machine profile targets one remote session; it does not combine every session on the host.

To use a named session instead, add the optional `--remote-session` flag:

```bash
herdr machine add workbox --label "Build machine" --remote-session agents
```

Machines that need explicit SSH settings can carry them in the profile:

```bash
herdr machine add server.example.com --label "Build machine" --user dev --port 2222 \
  --identity-file ~/.ssh/build --identities-only --proxy-jump bastion --color blue --group prod
```

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Add a machine
chunks.text:
The connection flags are `--port`, `--user`, `--identity-file` (repeatable), `--identities-only`, `--identity-agent`, `--strict-host-key-checking ask|accept-new|yes`, `--proxy-jump` (repeatable; either a target such as `user@host:port` or `profile:<id>` to hop through another saved machine), `--forward-agent`, `--server-alive-interval`, `--server-alive-count-max`, `--control-persist`, and `--remote-command`. `--group`, `--tag` (repeatable), and `--color` (hex or named color) are organization metadata for list output and the sidebar. All flags are optional; a machine without them connects exactly as before. Profile connection settings are written into Herdr's generated SSH config after your own SSH config is included, so per-option, settings from your `~/.ssh/config` win and the profile only fills gaps. Background connections still never prompt; authentication behavior is unchanged. `--remote-command` overrides the command SSH executes and therefore does not work with Herdr's bridge startup.

The host-key policy deserves a note of its own, because background connections cannot ask you anything. Without a profile setting, saved machines keep the historical behavior: `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`, so the host key must already be in your `known_hosts` (first connections to an unknown host fail with Attention). A profile's policy is passed to background SSH on the command line, so it takes effect even when your SSH config says something different:

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Add a machine
chunks.text:
- `accept-new` records a previously unknown host key on first connect (trust on first use) and keeps rejecting changed keys afterwards. This is the convenient choice for a new machine you already trust by other means.
- `ask` behaves as `yes` in the background: there is no terminal to answer the prompt, so unknown keys are still refused.
- `yes` keeps strict checking against your existing `known_hosts`.

To pre-seed or repair `known_hosts` yourself (for example before switching a profile from `accept-new` back to `yes`), use the standard OpenSSH tools:

```bash
ssh-keyscan server.example.com >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts   # record current keys
ssh-keygen -F server.example.com                        # show recorded fingerprints
ssh-keygen -R server.example.com                        # forget recorded keys (e.g. after a reimage)
```

Herdr checks both the installed binary and the running server. It starts the requested background server before saving the profile. Compatible client and server versions do not have to match. Missing or incompatible installations go through an approval-based setup. When the running server needs replacement, setup asks before stopping it and its pane processes, then starts the compatible server. The default answer is No. If installation and replacement are both needed, one confirmation covers them. `machine add` does not use experimental live handoff. Cancelling or failing setup leaves the profile unsaved.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Add a machine
chunks.text: Run `herdr` to open the UI. If a local client is already open, added and enabled machines normally appear within a second and connect in the background without changing your selection. An in-progress machine switch finishes before profile changes are applied. The remote server keeps running after setup exits.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Add a machine
chunks.text: You can also add a machine without leaving the UI: open the machines page from the global menu or with `prefix+m`, then press `a`. The wizard walks through target and label, connection fields (user, port, identity files, proxy jumps, host-key policy, and more), session and organization (group, tags, color), and a confirm page. The confirm page pre-authorizes the same installation, update, or required server restart that `machine add` would ask about in a terminal, and the wizard then shows each setup step as it runs: platform detection, install or update, server start, and endpoint verification. SSH still runs non-interactively inside the UI, so key-based authentication must already work, and the host key must already be accepted unless the profile's policy is `accept-new`; a failed step names the failing phase, prints the standalone command (for example `herdr --remote workbox`) that completes the setup in an interactive terminal, and offers two in-UI recovery entries: a host-key review that scans and records the presented key after your confirmation, and an approved interactive authentication attempt that verifies credentials through the askpass channel before you retry the setup. A machine is only saved after setup succeeds.

## Connection problems

- **Reconnecting:** Herdr retries automatically after a network interruption, sleep, or SSH failure. Repeated failures increase the delay up to two minutes; brief successful connections do not reset it. A connection must remain healthy for a minute before the next interruption gets a fast retry. The banner on the affected machine shows the reconnect attempt count and the estimated next attempt, with clickable actions: **retry now** schedules an immediate attempt, and **give up** disables the machine (re-enable it from the machines page). SSH connections are checked for application-level activity and probed when quiet, so a broken connection does not stay Online indefinitely. Local detects native connection closure or failure instead of using remote health probes.
- **Attention:** The target needs an action that cannot be completed in the background, such as host-key approval, authentication, or a compatible server. Other machines remain usable. The attention marker stays on the machine's sidebar row; clicking it opens that machine's detail card with a structured failure reason (DNS, timeout, unknown or changed host key, authentication, remote install, protocol), the suggested next step, the standalone fix command, and a reconnect action. Failures that have an in-UI recovery path also show a **review** button:

- *Unknown host key* opens a trust-on-first-use dialog showing the host, key type, and SHA256 fingerprint (scanned first when the failure did not capture one). Compare the fingerprint out of band, then choose **trust & remember** (records the key into `known_hosts` and reconnects), **this time only** (reconnects once with a process-local `accept-new` override that is never written to the catalog), or **abort**.
  - *Changed host key* opens a hard-blocking dialog that separates the reimage case from a possible man-in-the-middle. Only after your out-of-band verification, **remove old key & retry** forgets the recorded key with `ssh-keygen -R` and reconnects, which then surfaces the new key through the unknown-key dialog.
  - *Authentication required* opens a guide listing the server-offered methods and the configured identity file. Approving **interactive auth** runs one interactive attempt through Herdr's in-memory askpass channel: SSH password and passphrase prompts surface as masked TUI input dialogs, answers travel only to the prompt responder and are never logged, stored, or persisted. A passphrase prompt also reminds you that `ssh-add` loads the key into the agent for future non-interactive connections. Alternatives on the same dialog pre-collect the host key or copy the standalone fix command. The wizard's failed setup offers the same interactive-auth and host-key review entries.

- **Saved-machine file error:** An unreadable or invalid catalog leaves current connections unchanged. Herdr shows a notice and automatically retries reading it.

When both installations support bridge idle cleanup, saved-machine connections to Linux and macOS also close their remote bridge after a minute without traffic in either direction. Sleep counts toward that deadline, which is checked when the host wakes. Quiet healthy connections exchange health checks; watching continuous output does not require typing. Cleanup leaves the remote Herdr server, sessions, and pane processes running. Older installations remain compatible without this optional cleanup.

Background connections never answer prompts or install, update, restart, or hand off a server. Interactive SSH authentication only ever runs after an explicit in-UI approval; the default path stays fully non-interactive and fails fast instead of prompting. For anything the in-UI recovery does not cover, run the standalone setup command shown by Herdr in an interactive terminal, for example:

```bash
herdr --remote workbox
```

Use your profile's target. If you chose a named session when adding it, include the optional `--session <name>` here too. Follow any approval prompts, then restart the client to retry the Attention connection. Do not stop a running server merely because its version differs from the client.
If authentication fails, check ordinary SSH first. For a passphrase-protected key, load it with `ssh-add` before starting Herdr's non-interactive background connections.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Import machines from your SSH config
chunks.text:
## Import machines from your SSH config

If your `~/.ssh/config` already describes your hosts, import them instead of retyping every setting:

```bash
herdr machine import                     # review the detected hosts and pick which to import
herdr machine import --yes               # import everything (required when stdin is not a terminal)
herdr machine import --host 'db-*' --group prod
herdr machine import --file ~/work/ssh_config
```

The import reads your SSH config, including `Include`d files, with OpenSSH semantics: the first value of each directive wins, `Host *` supplies the fallback, and host matching is case-insensitive with `*`/`?` wildcards and `!` negation. `Match` blocks cannot be evaluated statically and are skipped. Your SSH config is only read, never modified.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Import machines from your SSH config
chunks.text: Each `Host` becomes a machine profile: the alias is the label, the resolved `HostName` the target, and `User`, `Port`, `IdentityFile`, `IdentitiesOnly`, `IdentityAgent`, `ProxyJump`, `ForwardAgent`, `ServerAliveInterval`, `ServerAliveCountMax`, `ControlPersist`, `RemoteCommand`, and `StrictHostKeyChecking` become profile fields — the same fields `machine add` accepts as flags. A `ProxyJump` hop that names another host imported in the same batch becomes a `profile:<id>` reference to it; other hops stay literal targets. Wildcard patterns such as `*.internal` are skipped unless you pass `--include-wildcards`; an imported wildcard profile is a template you edit before use. Hosts duplicating a saved machine's label or target — or each other — are skipped and reported per host, so re-running an import is safe.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Import machines from your SSH config
chunks.text:
The same import runs inside the UI: on the machines page press `i` (or use the command palette's "import machines from SSH config") to open a wizard that lists the detected hosts with the ones it will skip and why, lets you check the hosts to import (space toggles, `a` selects all or none, and a group field assigns one group to the batch), and reports each host as imported, skipped, or failed with its reason. Imported machines connect in the background exactly like the CLI path; remote server setup stays an explicit step. The selection step scrolls when the config holds more hosts than fit on screen — the wildcard toggle, the group field, and the counter stay pinned to the bottom — and the result step scrolls with the arrow keys so the last host is always reachable.

Import only registers profiles; it never installs, updates, or restarts a remote server. Imported machines connect in the background afterwards, and a machine that needs setup shows Attention with its standalone setup command. To register a single host with the same preparation `machine add` performs, use:

```bash
herdr machine add --from-config web
```

This resolves `web` in your SSH config, registers it with the full directives found there, and runs the usual remote setup before saving. Connection-option flags cannot be combined with `--from-config`; `--label`, `--remote-session`, `--group`, `--tag`, and `--color` still apply.

## Input broadcast

Broadcasting sends what you type into one pane to a registered set of panes — one per endpoint (Local or a saved machine) — so the same command runs everywhere at once. Because mistyped input would fan out too, the mechanism is gated twice: the set starts empty and disabled, and nothing is sent until the set is non-empty and explicitly enabled.

Manage the set in the UI from the machines page (`b` on the list or the detail card, or the command palette's "broadcast input…"): `g` toggles broadcasting on and off, `a` walks through picking a machine and then one of its online panes, `x` removes the selected target, and `c` clears the set. The set persists in `broadcast.json` next to the endpoint catalog and is shared with the CLI (`herdr broadcast status/enable/disable/add/remove/clear/send`; see [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference/#input-broadcast)).

While broadcasting is live, the mode bar carries a permanent `⇄ BROADCAST ×N` badge — even in plain terminal mode — so you never type into a fan-out unknowingly. Typed text and key presses go to every registered pane through the per-endpoint API channels; the pane you are typing into is excluded (it already has the input), pastes keep the target's own bracketed-paste handling, and mouse input is never broadcast. A target that rejects input reports once in a toast and re-arms after the next success; offline targets are skipped. Turn it off from the same overlay (`g` again) or with `herdr broadcast disable`.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Inspect and run one-off commands
chunks.text:
## Inspect and run one-off commands

Two CLI commands cover quick checks without opening the UI:

```bash
herdr machine status "Build machine" [--json]
herdr machine exec "Build machine" -- systemctl --user status herdr
```

`machine status` resolves a label or profile id (disabled machines included) and reports the profile, a live connection probe with its structured failure kind when the machine is unreachable, the remote server version and protocol compatibility when online, the saved port forward rules, and the session-log preferences. `machine exec` runs a single remote command over the same managed SSH channel as the file operations: stdio passes through to your terminal and the remote exit status becomes the command's, with no prompting and no timeout. Everything after the `--` separator is the remote command verbatim.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Pages and authentication recovery
chunks.text:
## Pages and authentication recovery

Wide terminals show machines and details side by side; narrow terminals open details from the list. The wizard preserves target, identity files, port, jump hosts, session, and display settings when returning from authentication. Review all settings by scrolling the confirmation page.

Approved interactive authentication uses an in-memory askpass channel through probing, installation, verification, and connection handover. Passwords are never persisted. Trust once pins the displayed key in a temporary known_hosts file owned by the connection. Permanent trust writes only the displayed key. `ssh -G` resolves the actual port, alias, and known_hosts paths. Proxy connections use OpenSSH's interactive verification over the same route when direct scanning is unavailable.

Canceling setup, authentication, or the file page terminates its local SSH/SCP/SFTP task. Completed remote writes are not rolled back. Stale directory reads are ignored while every request is settled, preventing stuck loading indicators.

Run `powershell -File scripts/windows_tui_compat.ps1 -ExePath target/debug/herdr.exe -Shell powershell` for PowerShell 5.1, or use `-Shell pwsh` for PowerShell 7. Add `-Interactive` inside WezTerm to check selection, IME, and 60×16, 80×24, 120×40, 160×50 layouts. In WSL, build and run Linux Herdr with the distribution's default user and login shell. CI checks ConPTY; desktop mouse and IME acceptance remain separate.

## Port forwarding

A saved machine can carry SSH port forward rules that start with its connection and restart when it reconnects. Manage the rules through the CLI, or in the UI from the machines list or the machine's detail card (`f` or the **forwards** button): the card lists the rules with their live status, and the rules page adds and removes them. The rules page scrolls to keep the selected rule visible, and `x` names the rule and waits for `enter` before deleting it (`esc` cancels). If the rules change while that prompt is up, the removal is cancelled rather than applied to whatever now sits in that position. Running clients pick up rule changes within about a second without reconnecting:

```bash
herdr machine forward list <profile-id>
herdr machine forward add <profile-id> --kind local --listen-port 8080 --target-host 127.0.0.1 --target-port 80
herdr machine forward add <profile-id> --kind remote --listen-port 9000 --target-host 127.0.0.1 --target-port 3000
herdr machine forward add <profile-id> --kind dynamic --listen-port 1080
herdr machine forward remove <profile-id> <rule-number>
```

The three kinds match `ssh -L`, `-R`, and `-D`:

- `local` listens on this machine (default bind `localhost`; override with `--bind-address`) and forwards through the SSH machine to `--target-host:--target-port`.
- `remote` listens on the SSH machine and forwards back to the target, which is reached from this machine.

- `dynamic` opens a local SOCKS proxy through the SSH machine and has no fixed target.

Each rule runs as its own non-interactive `ssh -N` child process over the same generated SSH config as the connection itself, so your `~/.ssh/config` still wins per option and forwarding never prompts. A rule that cannot start — for example because the local listen port is already taken — fails only that rule; the reason is recorded with it, shown next to the rule on the machine's detail card and rules page, and the connection and other rules are unaffected. A machine accepts up to 16 rules.

## Remote files

Every saved machine also exposes its filesystem through the same managed SSH channel, using the OpenSSH `sftp` client in batch mode. This is meant for small files — configs, scripts, notes — not bulk transfer:

These one-off channels share a single ssh control connection (a master) per saved profile, so consecutive file operations skip the TCP and SSH handshake; it idles out after `ControlPersist` (120 seconds by default, overridable per profile). The reusable config directory lives under `/tmp/herdr-ssh-<uid>-*` with owner and permission checks, and editing a profile's connection fields switches to a fresh master immediately.

```bash
herdr machine fs build ls /srv/app
herdr machine fs build stat /srv/app/config.toml
herdr machine fs build cat /srv/app/config.toml
herdr machine fs build get /srv/app/config.toml ./config.toml
herdr machine fs build put ./notes.txt /srv/app/notes.txt
herdr machine fs build mkdir /srv/app/logs --parents
herdr machine fs build mv /srv/app/notes.txt /srv/app/notes-old.txt
herdr machine fs build rm /srv/app/notes-old.txt
herdr machine fs build rm /srv/app/old-logs --recursive
```

The profile selector accepts a label or profile id, exactly like the global `--machine` prefix. Operations reuse the profile's generated SSH config, connection multiplexing, and non-interactive option family, so your `~/.ssh/config` keeps winning per option and nothing ever prompts. Remote paths are resolved by the sftp server relative to the login directory (`~` is not expanded); paths that start with `-` are rejected so they cannot be read as flags, and paths containing `\` or `"` are rejected because batch quoting for them is inconsistent across OpenSSH versions. `ls` and `stat` accept `--json`.

Transfers are capped at 1 MiB per file. `get` writes the local file atomically with `0600` permissions and never replaces through a symlink; `put` uploads to a sibling temporary name and renames it over the target atomically, restoring the previous permission bits when the target already existed. `mkdir --parents` creates intermediate directories; `rm` on a directory requires `--recursive`, never follows symlinks, and refuses the remote root. A changed SSH transport (auth, host key, DNS, timeout) surfaces through the same structured failure kinds as the connection itself, so a broken machine reports Attention in the UI instead of hanging the command.

The same channel drives the in-UI file browser: from the machines list or a machine's detail card press `o` (or the **files** button) to open it. The browser lists the remote directory with kind, size, and modified time; Enter descends into a directory or opens a file in the read-only viewer (small files up to 1 MiB), Backspace goes up, `r` refreshes, and `/` filters the listing. `d` downloads the selected file to a local path you confirm, `u` uploads a local file into the current directory, `m` creates a directory, `R` renames, and `x` deletes after a confirmation (directories delete recursively). Operations run on background workers and report errors inline, so the UI never blocks on SSH.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Rename, disable, or remove
chunks.text:
## Rename, disable, or remove

Read profile IDs from the list rather than deriving them from labels or hostnames:

```bash
herdr machine list
herdr machine rename <profile-id> --label "New name"
herdr machine disable <profile-id>
herdr machine enable <profile-id>
herdr machine remove <profile-id>
```

For scripts, add `--json` to `machine list`.

Renaming changes the displayed label without reconnecting. Disabling keeps the profile for later; removing forgets it. Both disconnect only that machine from the client and leave its remote sessions and agents running, even if the host is unreachable.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Rename, disable, or remove
chunks.text: The same operations are available in the UI. Open the machines page from the global menu or with `prefix+m` to see every saved machine with its live status, target, group, and server version. Press Enter for the detail card, which lists the full profile (including all connection fields), the machine's port forward rules with their live status, and, after a failed connection, a structured failure reason with the suggested next step and a review entry when the failure has an in-UI recovery (see [Connection problems](#connection-problems)). From the list or the card you can rename (`R`), edit the profile (`e`: group, tags, color, session, and the connection fields), enable or disable (`d`), remove after a confirmation (`x`), trigger an immediate reconnect (`r`), open the port forward rules (`f`) or the remote file browser (`o`), review a failure (`v`), and copy the fix command (`c`) — the same keys in both places, always acting on the keyboard selection. One-shot feedback such as "fix command copied" shows at the bottom of the machine list and of a machine's detail card, and clears itself after a few seconds. Right-clicking a machine in the sidebar offers the same actions plus a "copy fix command" entry that puts the machine's standalone setup command on the clipboard and confirms with a notification when the machines page is not open. Editing a machine's session or connection fields reconnects only that machine. The list also offers **import** (`i`, the import button, or the command palette's "import machines from SSH config"), which opens the same SSH config import as `machine import` as a three-step wizard, and the card's **forwards** entry (`f`) manages port forward rules with their live status.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Rename, disable, or remove
chunks.text: Removing or disabling the machine you are viewing returns you to Local. If Local is unavailable, Herdr shows that and retries its connection instead of selecting a different remote machine. With enabled saved machines, the client can remain usable even if Local fails or restarts.

## Scene snapshots

A scene snapshot captures the current working scene so you can restore it later with one action: the enabled machine set, the active machine with its workspace and tab (recorded per machine where the client has a cached view), and the sidebar chrome (width, collapsed state, and collapsed groups). Open the snapshots page from the command palette ("save scene…" / "restore scene") and press `s` to save the current scene under a name with an optional note. Up to 32 scenes are kept in a versioned `scene-snapshots.json` next to the endpoint catalog.

Restoring a scene enables the machines it recorded. The "disable machines outside the scene" toggle (`x`) is **off by default**: a plain restore never switches off machines the snapshot does not name. Turn it on and the restore first shows a confirmation naming every machine it would disable and disconnect — the confirmation key there is `y` (or `ctrl+↵`), not `↵`, so a held or double-tapped Enter can never walk through it, and only the machines that confirmation listed are switched off. Nothing is written to the endpoint catalog until you confirm; when the scene already covers every enabled machine there is nothing to disable and the restore runs straight away. The recorded active machine and its workspace become the selection when they are online, and online background machines get their recorded workspace focused as well. A machine the snapshot names but the catalog no longer has does not fail the restore; it is skipped and listed in the result toast.

In the scene list a single click only selects a row — restore runs from the "restore" button, from `Enter`, or from a second click on the same row. Scenes can be renamed and deleted from the same page. Scene names are unique: both saving and renaming under a name another scene already uses are rejected with an inline error instead of dropping either snapshot.

## Session logs

A machine profile can mirror its panes into local log files — useful for audit trails or reviewing what an agent did while you were elsewhere:

```bash
herdr machine log <profile-id> on
herdr machine log <profile-id> on --path "{machine}/{date}-{pane}.log" --max-bytes 16777216 --interval 30
herdr machine log <profile-id> show
herdr machine log <profile-id> dump
herdr machine log <profile-id> off
```

The mechanism is snapshot-based, by design. A client-side worker polls the machine's panes through its JSON API bridge on the configured interval (default 30 seconds) and appends a snapshot whenever a pane's revision changes — a separator line with the UTC timestamp, machine, pane, and revision, followed by up to 200 lines of the pane's recent text. This is not a continuous byte stream: rapid output between two polls is represented by its latest state, like a periodic `pane read`. The worker keeps its own bridge, so logging does not depend on which machine you are viewing, and it restarts with the machine's connection lifecycle.

Paths come from a template with `{date}` (UTC day), `{machine}` (label slug), `{machine-id}`, `{pane}`, and `{session}` variables; relative templates resolve under `<state dir>/session-logs/`. The default is `{machine}/{date}-{pane}.log`. Files are created with private permissions and rotate to `<file>.1` at the size cap (default 16 MiB). All writes go through a single background queue — a slow disk or a flooding pane never blocks the client; snapshots that would overflow the queue are dropped and counted rather than back-pressuring the UI. Toggling logging edits only the profile's `session_log` field, so it never reconnects the machine. `dump` runs exactly one snapshot cycle immediately and reports how many snapshots were appended, which is the fastest way to verify a template.

The same preferences are editable in the UI: the machines page edit form ends with the session log fields — an on/off/default choice plus the path template, size cap, and interval (empty keeps the defaults). Leaving the choice at **default** preserves the saved value untouched, so editing other fields never drops an existing configuration. The machine's detail card shows the effective template, cap, and interval, and, while logging is on, the writer queue's dropped-snapshot counter when it is non-zero.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Settings and automation
chunks.text:
## Settings and automation

The UI uses the client's local theme, sidebar settings, and keybindings by default. Custom commands and plugins advertised by the selected server still run there. Herdr does not copy local command plugins, configuration, executables, or secrets onto SSH hosts. Missing remote commands fail visibly. Use the UI's `reload config` action after editing client settings; see [Configuration](/docs/configuration/#reload-config).

Default agent rows show a `machine` token when multiple machines are present. Existing custom rows are preserved; add `machine` explicitly if you want that label in your layout. [Sidebar row layouts](/docs/configuration/#sidebar-row-layouts) also support conditional colors for machine labels.

Workspace, tab, pane IDs, and agent names are scoped to one server. Two machines may both contain `w1:p1` or an agent named `reviewer`. Selecting a machine in the UI does not retarget CLI commands running in an existing pane: they still use that pane's inherited session and socket. For remote automation, use `herdr --machine <label-or-id> agent list`, then pass the same prefix when controlling those remote IDs. The CLI uses the saved profile's SSH target and session directly; it does not need an open TUI. Without `--machine`, existing session/socket routing is unchanged. See [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference/#saved-ssh-machines) for supported commands, update requirements, and remote path rules.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Switch between machines
chunks.text:
## Switch between machines

Choose a machine or one of its workspaces in the sidebar. The selected machine receives your pane input and terminal size, and supplies the visible terminal content and graphics. Other connected machines keep updating their workspace information, agent states, and notifications without streaming their pane screens.

Machines with a `group` in their profile are listed under that group in the sidebar; ungrouped machines keep their saved order. Each machine row carries a color tag on the left — the profile's `color` when set, otherwise a stable color derived from its label. In the compact (collapsed) sidebar the row is four cells wide, so the tag moves onto the machine's first letter, which takes the same color.

Click the arrow beside any machine to collapse or expand its workspace list without switching away from your current workspace. This also works while that machine is reconnecting.

For keyboard navigation, press `prefix+w`, then use the workspace navigation keys (Up/Down by default) to highlight workspaces across connected machines in sidebar order. Enter activates the highlighted workspace; Esc or the prefix key cancels without switching. Compact and expanded sidebars reveal the highlighted row, including under a collapsed machine. On desktop, navigation wraps at the ends; the mobile switcher stops at the first or last workspace. Disconnected machines are skipped.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Switch between machines
chunks.text:
When highlighting a workspace on another machine, press Enter before using other keyboard actions. This prevents pane, tab, workspace, or custom-command shortcuts from acting on the current machine by mistake. Clicking cancels a remote desktop keyboard preview. Expanded sidebars respect each machine's collapsed worktree groups.

Local opens immediately on startup without waiting for SSH connections. A stalled machine cannot hold up another machine's input. Multiple Herdr clients can also view different tabs on the same server independently; see [Client and server](/docs/concepts/#client-and-server) for shared-tab sizing.

When a connection is lost, the last workspace and agent state remains visible but dimmed. That is cached information, not live state. Input and navigation into those cached panes stay disabled until a fresh connection and matching screen arrive. Reconnecting never takes selection away from the machine you are using.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Switch between machines
chunks.text: This lockout is deliberate. While the link is down the client cannot verify the session's state, so typed input could land in the wrong context — a shell that has moved on, a different prompt, an agent mid-task. Disabling pane input and dimming the cached screen makes that boundary explicit instead of letting keystrokes drift into an uncertain session. Nothing is lost on the other side: the remote Herdr server keeps the session, its agents, and its pane processes intact while the link is down, and the workspace resumes as it was once a fresh connection arrives. If you do not want to wait for the automatic backoff, the reconnect banner on the affected machine offers two actions: **retry now** runs an immediate attempt, and **give up** disables the machine (re-enable it from the machines page).

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Updates and saved data
chunks.text:
## Updates and saved data

Saved profiles contain an opaque ID, label, SSH target, explicit remote session, and enabled state, plus any optional organization metadata (group, tags, color), SSH connection options (port, user, identity files, proxy jumps, and similar) set at `machine add` time, port forward rules, and session-log preferences. Herdr does not store passwords, private keys, agent tickets, or SSH control sockets in the catalog. Authentication stays with OpenSSH. The catalog file is versioned; this release upgrades it from version 1 to version 2 automatically on first load, and older Herdr versions cannot read a version 2 catalog.

The client and server negotiate compatibility rather than requiring identical versions. Saved-machine connections additionally need the server's `surface_interest` and `health_check` capabilities. Older servers without those capabilities show Attention until explicitly updated, even if a standalone attach works. Other missing server methods disable only their corresponding actions.

Updating a compatible client does not replace the running remote server or stop its agents. When you need new server-side behavior, update that server explicitly. Normal replacement asks before stopping the server and its pane processes.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Updates and saved data
chunks.text: Live handoff is experimental and opt-in. For a supported server that needs replacement during standalone setup, you can explicitly add `--handoff` to `herdr --remote`; it is not needed for normal connections or authentication fixes. See [Update](/docs/install/#update) for restart and handoff choices, and [Session state and restore](/docs/session-state/) for what survives each operation.

chunks.anchor: Before you connect > Why not mosh
chunks.text:
## Why not mosh

mosh is built for interactive terminal sessions: it synchronizes screen state and keystrokes over UDP using its own terminal emulator on the server side. Herdr's remote transport is something else entirely — an SSH stdio pipe that carries Herdr's binary wire protocol (length-prefixed structured messages: requests, responses, events, and frames) between the client and a resident remote Herdr server. mosh cannot carry that: it offers no general byte-stream channel, only screen synchronization, and its server component only starts terminal sessions.

More importantly, the resilience mosh provides is already built into Herdr at a different layer. A remote Herdr server owns the session state — panes, agents, workspaces — and keeps running when the network drops. The client supervisor detects a broken transport (application-level health checks, not just TCP), reconnects with backoff, and reuses SSH connection multiplexing so reconnects are cheap; wake-from-sleep and network changes are just another reconnect. Nothing about the session depends on the transport staying up, which is exactly the property mosh adds to a plain shell. Adding UDP-based mosh underneath would instead weaken the model: it requires a `mosh-server` binary on the host and open UDP, neither of which SSH-only environments provide. The transport therefore stays plain SSH everywhere, including for the JSON API channel used by remote automation.

---
title: Connecting machines
description: Work across Local and saved SSH machines in one Herdr window, with shared agent navigation and independent reconnects.
---

Keep your local work and remote agents in one Herdr window. Save an SSH machine once, then switch between its workspaces and Local without opening another client. The agent list includes connected machines, so you can see where work is running and which agent needs an answer.

Each machine keeps its own Herdr server, sessions, and running processes. A lost connection to one machine does not disconnect the others.

## Local work

Start Herdr from the project directory:

```bash
herdr
```

Herdr starts or attaches to your local background session automatically. You do not manage sockets. Run shells, servers, tests, and agents normally inside panes.

Detach the client with `ctrl+b q`. Your panes keep running.

Reattach later:

```bash
herdr
```

If you want to end the session and stop its panes, stop the server:

```bash
herdr server stop
```

chunks.anchor: Local work > Remote work from your local terminal
chunks.text:
## Remote work from your local terminal

Attach through SSH without opening a shell first:

```bash
herdr --remote workbox
herdr --remote ssh://you@server:2222
```

The remote server keeps the panes running and sends their terminal content and session state over SSH. Your local Herdr draws the UI using your local theme and presentation settings.

Use this path when you want the remote session to feel local. The client runs on your machine, so local desktop features such as image clipboard paste can be bridged to the remote server. If you SSH first and run `herdr` on the server, Herdr runs entirely on that server and cannot read your local desktop clipboard.

For repeat targets, put the host in your SSH config:

```text
Host workbox
  HostName server.example.com
  User you
  Port 2222
```

Then attach with:

```bash
herdr --remote workbox
```

chunks.anchor: Local work > Remote work through normal SSH
chunks.text:
## Remote work through normal SSH

SSH to the machine that has the code and credentials, then run Herdr there:

```bash
ssh you@server
herdr
```

This works like a terminal multiplexer. Your shell is remote. The Herdr server is remote. The agents and panes run on the remote machine. Detach with `ctrl+b q`, disconnect, then SSH back and run `herdr` again.

Use this path when you already live inside an SSH shell, when you are on a phone or tablet SSH client, or when you want the simplest setup.

chunks.anchor: Local work > Which path to use
chunks.text:
## Which path to use

Use `herdr` for local work. Use `ssh you@server` then `herdr` when you want Herdr to behave like tmux on that remote shell or when you are using a phone SSH client. Use `herdr --remote <host>` for a local UI attached to one remote session, including local clipboard image paste. To keep Local and several SSH machines in one window, save them with `herdr machine add <host> --label <label>`; see [Connecting machines](/docs/connecting-machines/).

For remote bootstrap details, named remote sessions, custom binaries, and direct terminal attach, see [Persistence and remote access](/docs/persistence-remote/).

chunks.anchor: Local work > Work from your phone
chunks.text: ## Work from your phone Herdr works on your phone without a mobile app or web dashboard. Install any SSH client, connect to the machine where your agents run, and start Herdr there: ```bash ssh you@server herdr ``` The same persistent Herdr session opens in your phone terminal. The TUI adapts to narrow screens, so you can inspect agents, switch workspaces, and check panes without leaving SSH. On iPhone, apps like [moshi](https://getmoshi.app/) work well.

---
title: How to work with Herdr
description: Run Herdr locally, inside SSH, or through remote attach.

Run Herdr where the work lives. Attach from wherever you are.

Herdr is a background session server plus one or more terminal clients. Panes keep running in the server. Clients attach, detach, and render the session.

chunks.anchor: Pick your path > Or let your agent introduce you
chunks.text:
## Or let your agent introduce you

If you already run an AI coding agent, let it handle the onboarding. Paste this prompt:

```text
Help me understand and set up Herdr. Read https://herdr.dev/agent-guide.md first, then walk me through it step by step.
```

The guide covers Herdr's concepts, setup, configuration, and common fixes, so your agent can answer from the docs instead of improvising.

import { Card, CardGrid } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

## Install

On Linux or macOS, run:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, run:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://herdr.dev/install.ps1 | iex"
```

If endpoint security blocks that fileless PowerShell command, open Command Prompt and run:

```cmd
curl.exe -fsSLo install.cmd https://herdr.dev/install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd
```

The installer downloads the release binary for your platform and places it on your PATH. New direct installs use the stable update channel. Existing Windows preview installs stay on preview until you switch them with `herdr channel set stable`. On Windows, PATH points to the active versioned release directory; the installer also updates the `current` and stable `bin` compatibility aliases, so updates do not need to overwrite a running `herdr.exe`.

## Download manually

You can also download a binary from [GitHub releases](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr/releases).

Choose the asset that matches your system:

| System | Asset |
| --- | --- |
| Linux x86_64 | `herdr-linux-x86_64` |
| Linux aarch64 | `herdr-linux-aarch64` |
| macOS Intel | `herdr-macos-x86_64` |
| macOS Apple silicon | `herdr-macos-aarch64` |
| Windows x86_64 | `herdr-windows-x86_64.zip` |

On Linux or macOS, make it executable and move it somewhere on your PATH.

```bash
chmod +x herdr-linux-x86_64
mv herdr-linux-x86_64 ~/.local/bin/herdr
```

### Windows archive

Stable releases and preview prereleases both include `herdr-windows-x86_64.zip`. The archive contains `herdr.exe` and its app-local ConPTY runtime. Keep the extracted directory together; do not copy only `herdr.exe`.

## Install with Homebrew

If you already use Homebrew:

```bash
brew install herdr
```

## Install with mise

If you already use mise:

```bash
mise use -g herdr
```

If mise reports `herdr not found in mise tool registry`, update mise and retry. Older mise versions predate the Herdr registry entry; `mise use -g github:herdrdev/herdr` works as a temporary fallback.

## Install with Nix

If you already use Nix, Herdr provides a flake that builds Herdr from source:

```bash
nix run github:herdrdev/herdr/v0.x.y
nix build github:herdrdev/herdr/v0.x.y
nix profile install github:herdrdev/herdr/v0.x.y
```

Replace `v0.x.y` with the latest release tag. You can omit the tag to track `master`, but release tags are recommended for normal installs.

The flake also exposes a development shell:

```bash
nix develop github:herdrdev/herdr
```

Use the same Nix workflow to update Herdr. For a profile install, list your profile entries and upgrade the Herdr entry:

```bash
nix profile list
nix profile upgrade <index-or-name>
```

If Herdr is an input in your own flake, update that input and rebuild your system, Home Manager, or development environment:

```bash
nix flake update herdr
```

## Requirements

Stable-channel binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows x86_64. See [Windows support](/docs/windows-beta/) for supported workflows and known limitations. Windows ARM64 runs the x86_64 build under Windows emulation.

## Update

Herdr checks for new releases and notifies you in the app. You can update manually:

```bash
herdr update
```

Use `herdr update` only for installs managed by Herdr's own installer. Update Homebrew, mise, and Nix installs through those package managers instead.

Direct installs on Linux, macOS, and Windows use the stable update channel by default. To opt into preview builds from `master`, set the channel:

```bash
herdr channel set preview
```

Switch a direct install back to stable the same way:

```bash
herdr channel set stable
```

For direct installs, changing channels checks the selected channel and installs its latest binary. If that update fails, run `herdr update` to retry from the configured channel.

Preview builds are regularly published GitHub prereleases from the current development branch. They are useful when you want fixes before the next stable release, but they can regress. Homebrew, mise, and Nix installs do not use the preview channel.

Stable is the recommended channel for normal Windows use. Preview receives fixes sooner but can regress, so opt in only when you want that tradeoff. Existing Windows preview installs remain on preview until you switch them explicitly. If an older preview build rejects `herdr channel set stable`, run `herdr update` once on preview, then retry the channel switch.

By default, `herdr update` installs the new binary and leaves endpoint-generation-1 servers and their pane processes running. Start Herdr again to reconnect with the updated client. Client-only changes work immediately. A new server-side action stays unavailable until that server is updated and restarted; the client shows a notice instead of disconnecting. Servers from before endpoint generation 1 need one final stop during update.

To opt into experimental live server handoff for supported running sessions, run:

```bash
herdr update --handoff
```

Live handoff does not apply to Homebrew, mise, or Nix package-manager updates. For those installs, update with the package manager, then run Herdr again to reconnect with the updated client. The compatible old server keeps running. Restart it later with `herdr server stop` or `herdr session stop <name>` only when you want server-side changes from the new release.

## Verify

Start Herdr:

```bash
herdr
```

If your shell cannot find `herdr`, restart the terminal or check that the install directory is on your PATH.

---
title: Install Herdr
description: Install, update, and verify Herdr on Linux, macOS, and Windows.
---

Herdr publishes stable-channel binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Windows is generally available, with documented platform-specific limitations and ongoing fixes.

## Install integrations

Open settings inside Herdr and use the integrations tab to install integrations for agents found on your `PATH`, or run commands manually. In that tab `Enter` (and the primary button) installs **only the row you have selected** — the primary button is shown only while the selected row actually needs one, and the footer lists `a`, which installs every pending integration at once:

```bash
herdr integration install pi
herdr integration install claude
herdr integration install codex
herdr integration install kimi
herdr integration install opencode
```

## Claude Code

Install the Claude Code hook:

```bash
herdr integration install claude
```

The hook reports Claude Code session identity to the local Herdr socket on session start. Claude Code state comes from Herdr's screen manifest detection.

Claude integration v10 matches only the documented `SessionStart` sources: `startup`, `resume`, `clear`, `compact`, and `fork`. This prevents third-party tools that import Claude hooks from firing the imported Herdr Claude hook on other source names, without disabling unrelated Claude-compatible hooks. Reinstall the Claude integration after upgrading to migrate the previous wildcard matcher. New Claude source values require an integration update.

Claude integration v11 also subscribes to `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop` (matcher `*`) and to `TaskCreated` and `TaskCompleted` on macOS and Linux. These hooks only tell the local Herdr socket that Claude Code's sub-agents or tasks changed; they do not report agent state. They are not installed on Windows. Reinstall the Claude integration after upgrading to add them.

Herdr uses `~/.claude` by default, or `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when set. The Claude config directory must already exist. Install writes `hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh` and updates `settings.json` with Herdr hook entries. Uninstall removes the matching hook entries and deletes the hook script.

## Codex

Install the Codex hook:

```bash
herdr integration install codex
```

The Codex hook reports session identity through the same local socket API used by other integrations. Codex state comes from Herdr's screen manifest detection.

Herdr uses `~/.codex` by default, or `CODEX_HOME` when set. The Codex config directory must already exist. Install writes `herdr-agent-state.sh`, updates `hooks.json`, and ensures `[features] hooks = true` in `config.toml`. It also removes the deprecated top-level `codex_hooks` flag when present. Uninstall removes Herdr entries from `hooks.json` and deletes the hook script, but leaves `config.toml` unchanged.

## Custom status labels

Integrations report lifecycle state as semantic state only. For example, report an agent as `working` without adding display fields to the lifecycle report.

```bash
herdr pane report-agent w1:p1 \
  --source custom:docs \
  --agent docs-bot \
  --state working
```

User hooks that run next to a Herdr-managed integration should use metadata instead of `report-agent`. Metadata changes presentation without taking over the integration's `idle`, `working`, `blocked`, or session restore authority. `--agent` and `--applies-to-source` guard only presentation fields (`--title`, `--display-agent`, and `--state-label`). Token patches always apply; their reporter owns clearing or TTL refresh. `--display-agent` changes the visible name.

```bash
herdr pane report-metadata "$HERDR_PANE_ID" \
  --source user:claude-title \
  --agent claude \
  --title "Refactor auth middleware" \
  --display-agent "Claude: auth" \
  --token summary="refactor auth" \
  --state-label working="refactoring auth" \
  --ttl-ms 3600000
```

Tokens and state labels are visual-only. Waits, notifications, and workspace rollups still use the semantic state.

## Debug integration state

List known agents:

```bash
herdr agent list
```

Read a pane when you need to verify what Herdr can see:

```bash
herdr pane read w1:p1 --source recent --lines 50
```

If integration state looks wrong, first confirm the agent is running inside Herdr and that the relevant hook or plugin was installed for the same user account.

chunks.anchor: Install integrations > How Herdr uses integrations
chunks.text:
## How Herdr uses integrations

Herdr uses integrations in two ways:

| Integration type | Agents | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifecycle authority | Pi, Kimi Code CLI, OpenCode | When installed and actively reporting for the pane, hook or plugin events author `idle`, `working`, and `blocked`. Herdr does not also use screen manifest fallback for that same lifecycle authority. |
| Session identity | Claude Code, Codex | The integration reports native session references for restore. State still comes from Herdr's screen manifest detection. |

Custom integrations can also report state that is not visible in the native terminal UI. They do not need to be built into Herdr or use a recognized agent executable.

chunks.anchor: Install integrations > Integrate your own agent
chunks.text:
## Integrate your own agent

An agent running in a Herdr pane inherits `HERDR_ENV`, `HERDR_PANE_ID`, `HERDR_BIN_PATH`, and `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`. If the agent exposes lifecycle hooks, use those hooks to report semantic state through Herdr's CLI:

```bash
"$HERDR_BIN_PATH" pane report-agent "$HERDR_PANE_ID" \
  --source custom:my-agent \
  --agent my-agent \
  --state working
```

Report `idle` when the agent is ready for input and `blocked` when it needs a user decision. Use `--message` to describe a block. When the agent exits, release the same source's lifecycle authority:

```bash
"$HERDR_BIN_PATH" pane release-agent "$HERDR_PANE_ID" \
  --source custom:my-agent \
  --agent my-agent
```

Report only when `HERDR_ENV=1` and the required variables are present. This keeps the integration a no-op outside Herdr. Keep `--source` stable and unique to the integration. If reports can arrive out of order, include a strictly increasing `--seq`; Herdr ignores stale sequence numbers from the same source.

You can include `--agent-session-id` or `--agent-session-path` with `report-agent`, or use `pane report-agent-session` when session identity changes independently of state. Herdr exposes that reference through its pane and agent APIs. Automatic session restore also requires Herdr to know how to launch that agent and resume the referenced session.

chunks.anchor: Install integrations > Integrate your own agent
chunks.text:
Use `HERDR_BIN_PATH` and the CLI wrappers for portable integrations. Code that needs direct IPC can send the equivalent `pane.report_agent`, `pane.report_agent_session`, and `pane.release_agent` requests described in the [Socket API](/docs/socket-api/#agent-state-reporting).

[Prime Agent's built-in Herdr reporter](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/builtin/herdr-agent-state.ts) is a real-world example. It activates only inside Herdr, maps agent events to `working`, `idle`, and `blocked`, preserves report ordering across sessions, and releases authority on exit.

Some integrations report native agent session references. Herdr uses official session references to resume Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code CLI, Pi, and OpenCode panes after a Herdr server restart unless `[session] resume_agents_on_restore = false` disables it.

Native session restore requires current Herdr integrations: Pi integration version `2`, Claude Code version `6`, Codex version `5`, Kimi Code CLI version `3`, or OpenCode version `5`. Check installed versions with `herdr integration status`.

## Kimi Code CLI

Install the Kimi Code CLI hook:

```bash
herdr integration install kimi
```

The hook reports Kimi session identity and lifecycle state to Herdr for native restore and authoritative `idle`, `working`, and `blocked` status. It requires Kimi Code CLI `0.14.0` or newer.

Herdr uses `~/.kimi-code` by default, or `KIMI_CODE_HOME` when set. The Kimi Code config directory must already exist. Install writes `hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh` and appends Herdr-managed `[[hooks]]` entries to `config.toml`. Uninstall removes the Herdr-managed config block and deletes the hook script.

Herdr resumes stored Kimi sessions with `kimi --session <id>`.

## OpenCode

Install the OpenCode plugin:

```bash
herdr integration install opencode
```

The integration supports OpenCode V1 `1.18.29` or later and OpenCode V2 (tested with beta `19242`). The OpenCode config directory must already exist. Herdr installs the server entrypoint at `~/.config/opencode/plugins/herdr-agent-state.js`, the shared TUI plugin at `herdr-tui-session.js`, and a V2 TUI entrypoint at `herdr-opencode/tui.js` in that config directory.

Install registers the V1 TUI plugin in `tui.jsonc` and the V2 TUI plugin in `cli.json`, preserving other preferences and plugins. If OpenCode still has V1 TUI preferences to import (`tui.json` or `kv.json`), Herdr defers registration so the first-start migration can run; start `opencode2` once and reinstall the integration afterward. Otherwise Herdr creates `cli.json` with the plugin registration. Restart the OpenCode TUI after installation. Uninstall removes the managed plugin files and their configuration entries.

V2 lifecycle reporting runs in the pane-local TUI, which associates events with its selected root session even when multiple panes share one OpenCode server. Completion and interruption clear the working state; pending permission requests, pending forms, and failed executions keep the pane blocked. V2 Mini and headless clients do not run the TUI plugin and therefore do not provide this lifecycle reporting.

The plugin reports lifecycle state and session identity while OpenCode runs inside a Herdr pane. After OpenCode emits a session-bearing event, Herdr can use the reported session id to resume the pane with `opencode --session <id>`. Native screen manifest detection remains available when the plugin is not installed.

## Pi

Install the Pi integration:

```bash
herdr integration install pi
```

Herdr writes the bundled extension to:

```text
~/.pi/agent/extensions/herdr-agent-state.ts
```

If `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` is set, Herdr writes to `$PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR/extensions/herdr-agent-state.ts` instead. Herdr creates the extensions directory when the Pi agent directory already exists. Uninstall removes only that extension file.

## Retired integrations

This fork ships official integrations for Pi, Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code CLI, and OpenCode only. Every other built-in integration has been retired, together with its bundled detection manifest:

- The CLI no longer accepts the retired names. `herdr integration install` and `herdr integration uninstall` answer a retired name such as `cursor` or `omp` with a retirement notice and the list of supported targets, and `herdr integration status` no longer lists them.
- Older clients can still send a retired target to the `integration.install` or `integration.uninstall` API methods. The request parses as before and is answered with the `integration_retired` error; `integration.list` no longer returns retired targets.
- Hooks or plugins that an earlier build installed into a retired agent's config directory are left untouched. Remove them by hand if you no longer want them; their session reports are treated as unofficial and are not used for restore. Since `herdr integration uninstall` also rejects retired names, this fork cannot remove them for you: open that agent's own config directory yourself and delete the hook or plugin file, using that agent's own documentation to find its exact location.
- A retired agent running in a pane is an ordinary program: it is not detected automatically, and config keys that named it (such as `[ui.sound.agents]` overrides) are ignored.

Any agent, retired or not, can still report state through the generic interface described in [Integrate your own agent](#integrate-your-own-agent). ZCode is planned to be supported as an external agent source rather than as a built-in integration.

## Uninstall integrations

```bash
herdr integration uninstall pi
herdr integration uninstall claude
herdr integration uninstall codex
herdr integration uninstall kimi
herdr integration uninstall opencode
```

Herdr saves integration configs atomically on Linux/macOS and for new files; existing Windows files keep their permissions through a backup-first, in-place update. If Windows reports a backup, close the agent and inspect the config before retrying: discard—not restore—an unfinished `.herdr-backup.pending` only after verifying the config, or restore completed `.herdr-backup` contents into the existing file if needed (if missing, establish its intended permissions first), then verify the config and remove the backup.

See [Monitoring, account usage and docking](/docs/monitoring/) for host metrics, provider account bindings, and movable terminal groups.


Herdr detects supported agents automatically. Install official integrations when you want native agent session restore, direct lifecycle reports, or both. See [Agents](/docs/agents/) for the full status authority model.

---
title: Keyboard
description: What the prefix is, which bindings to learn first, and how to go prefix-free.
---

:::tip[Coming from tmux or zellij?]
You already know this model. Jump to the [keybinding reference](/docs/configuration/#keybindings) for the full default keymap and config syntax.
:::

Herdr is mouse-native. You can click panes, tabs, workspaces, and agents, drag split borders, and use right-click menus without learning a single keybinding. Keyboard control is optional. In floating overlays the wheel scrolls the viewport without moving the keyboard selection, and the wheel step is `ui.mouse_scroll_lines` (3 by default) for panes, sidebar lists, and overlays alike.

chunks.anchor: What the prefix is > Change anything
chunks.text:
## Change anything

Every binding is configurable, including the prefix itself:

```toml
[keys]
prefix = "ctrl+a"
```

chunks.anchor: What the prefix is > Copy mode
chunks.text:
## Copy mode

Press `prefix+[` to enter copy mode for the focused pane. Use `h/j/k/l`, tmux-style `w/b/e` and big-word `W/B/E`, `{`/`}`, `PageUp`/`PageDown`, `ctrl+b`/`ctrl+f`, and `ctrl+u`/`ctrl+d` to move. Press `/` or `?` for forward or backward literal search, then `n` or `N` to repeat in the same or opposite direction. Search is case-insensitive unless the query contains an uppercase letter. Use `v` or Space to start a selection, `y` or Enter to copy it, and `q` or Esc to leave without copying. Esc clears an active selection or search before exiting. Copy mode does not pause the pane process: output remains live, follows at the bottom, and stays pinned when you navigate into history. The configured prefix keeps its normal meaning in copy mode; with the default prefix, `ctrl+b` enters prefix mode instead of paging up, so use a different prefix if you want `ctrl+b` for copy-mode page-up. Mouse drag-select copies without entering copy mode at all.

chunks.anchor: What the prefix is > Going prefix-free
chunks.text:
## Going prefix-free

You can bind Herdr actions to direct chords that need no prefix at all. The hard part is knowing which chords are safe, because terminals, shells, and desktop environments already own most of the keyboard.

Any chord works as a binding: `ctrl+j`, `alt+k`, whatever fits your hands. But a chord has to survive three layers before Herdr sees it: your operating system, your outer terminal (Ghostty, iTerm2, and others ship their own defaults), and the programs running inside the pane. `ctrl+j` reaches Herdr fine, but shells and editors treat it as enter. `alt+k` is free on Linux, but macOS composes it into a special character in most terminals. If you pick chords from these families, double-check them against your own terminal and OS shortcuts.

We mapped the default keybindings of Ghostty, iTerm2, Terminal.app, kitty, WezTerm, Alacritty, Warp, Windows Terminal, GNOME Terminal, and Konsole, plus the global shortcuts of GNOME and KDE. One modifier family is almost untouched everywhere: `ctrl+alt`. Terminals leave it free, it is not affected by the macOS option-key composing behavior that blocks plain `alt` chords, and it transmits even in terminals without a modern keyboard protocol. It is a safe default, but the choice is yours.

This setup keeps the prefix bindings working and adds direct chords on top:

```toml
[keys]
focus_pane_left = ["prefix+h", "ctrl+alt+h"]
focus_pane_down = ["prefix+j", "ctrl+alt+j"]
focus_pane_up = ["prefix+k", "ctrl+alt+k"]

chunks.anchor: What the prefix is > Going prefix-free
chunks.text:
focus_pane_right = ["prefix+l", "ctrl+alt+l"]
previous_tab = ["prefix+p", "ctrl+alt+["]
next_tab = ["prefix+n", "ctrl+alt+]"]
new_tab = ["prefix+c", "ctrl+alt+c"]
split_vertical = ["prefix+v", "ctrl+alt+d"]
split_horizontal = ["prefix+minus", "ctrl+alt+shift+d"]
zoom = ["prefix+z", "ctrl+alt+z"]
```

A few `ctrl+alt` chords are taken elsewhere. Avoid these:

| Chord | Owned by |
| --- | --- |
| `ctrl+alt+arrows` | GNOME workspace switching, Ghostty and Konsole defaults |
| `ctrl+alt+t` | "Launch terminal" on Ubuntu and Fedora |
| `ctrl+alt+l` / `ctrl+alt+a` | KDE lock screen / attention window |
| `ctrl+alt+s` / `ctrl+alt+u` | Konsole |
| `ctrl+alt+f1..f12` | Linux virtual console switching |

If a direct chord does nothing, your terminal or desktop environment consumed it before Herdr could see it. Rebind either side: free the chord in the terminal's settings, or pick another chord in Herdr.

chunks.anchor: What the prefix is > Learn these five first
chunks.text:
## Learn these five first

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| New tab | `prefix+c` |
| Split right / down | `prefix+v` / `prefix+minus` |
| Move between panes | `prefix+h/j/k/l` |
| Workspace navigation | `prefix+w` |
| Detach, leave everything running | `prefix+q` |

These cover most daily movement. Everything else can stay on the mouse.

## What the prefix is

A terminal multiplexer sits between your terminal and the programs running inside it. Those programs already use most key combinations: `ctrl+c` interrupts, `ctrl+r` searches history, editors claim nearly everything else. If Herdr grabbed common keys directly, it would break the programs inside it.

The prefix solves this. Press the prefix key, default `ctrl+b`, and the next keypress goes to Herdr instead of your terminal. `prefix+c` means: press `ctrl+b`, release, then press `c`. Herdr reserves one key instead of dozens.

Press `prefix+?` at any time to see every active binding. Press `/` in the keybind help to filter actions and shortcuts; use Backspace to edit the filter or `ctrl+u` to clear it. While prefix mode waits for the next key, a which-key popup lists the bindings available next (set `ui.which_key = false` to disable it). The menu button in the sidebar footer opens a fuzzy command palette over every action — including machine connect, edit, and SSH config import, plus snippet management and runs, scene snapshots, and the input broadcast manager — that surfaces recently used commands when the search box is empty.

Overlay pages carry their own local keys, shown in each page's footer: on the machines page (`prefix+m`), `b` opens the broadcast target set, and the machine actions — `e` edit, `R` rename, `r` reconnect, `f` port forwards, `o` remote file browser, `d` enable/disable, `x` remove, `v` review a failure, `c` copy the fix command — work the same from the list and from a machine's detail card. One-shot feedback such as "fix command copied" appears at the bottom of the machine list and of a machine's detail card, and clears itself after a few seconds. While input broadcast is on, the mode bar shows a permanent `⇄ BROADCAST ×N` badge so you can never miss that your typing fans out to other machines.

chunks.anchor: What the prefix is > The rest, by task
chunks.text:
## The rest, by task

Panes:

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Zoom the focused pane | `prefix+z` |
| Close pane | `prefix+x` |
| Swap panes | `prefix+shift+h/j/k/l` |
| Resize mode | `prefix+r` |
| Copy mode | `prefix+[` |
| Link hints (two-letter markers over visible URLs) | `prefix+u` |

Tabs:

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Next / previous tab | `prefix+n` / `prefix+p` |
| Jump to tab 1–9 | `prefix+1..9` |
| Rename tab | `prefix+shift+t` |
| Close tab | `prefix+shift+x` |

Workspaces and session:

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| New workspace | `prefix+shift+n` |
| Rename workspace | `prefix+shift+w` |
| Close workspace | `prefix+shift+d` |
| Goto picker | `prefix+g` |
| Toggle sidebar | `prefix+b` |

The Goto picker (`prefix+g`) is the session navigator. Its search box splits your query on whitespace and keeps a row only when every word appears somewhere in it, so `server web` finds `web server` and word order no longer matters. While a search or status filter is active the selection starts on the first row that matched, instead of on the workspace row that was only pulled in to hold it, so Enter opens what you searched for. Home still returns to the top of the list. (`prefix+w` is a different key: it moves the sidebar into workspace-navigation mode and has no search box.)

The full keymap and the binding syntax live in the [keybinding reference](/docs/configuration/#keybindings).

## Browse plugins

The [marketplace](/plugins/) lists public repositories tagged with the GitHub
topic `herdr-plugin` when their default branch contains at least one
`herdr-plugin.toml` whose required metadata can be parsed. Search by repository
or plugin metadata, and sort repository cards by popularity, recent activity,
or newest. Each card links to its source repository and lists every discovered
plugin inside it.

Discovery is automatic and unreviewed. A listing means a repository tagged
itself, not that Herdr vetted it, so the
[trust guidance](/docs/plugins/#trust-and-security) applies before you install
anything.

chunks.anchor: Browse plugins > Get your plugin listed
chunks.text:
## Get your plugin listed

Add the GitHub topic `herdr-plugin` to a public repository and put one or more
`herdr-plugin.toml` manifests with parseable required metadata on its default
branch. Manifests may be at the root or in subdirectories. The marketplace uses
one card per repository and lists each valid manifest as a separately
installable plugin. The index refreshes automatically every 30 minutes and
rescans repositories when their default-branch head changes.

## Install a plugin

The marketplace helps you discover plugins. Install any plugin straight from
GitHub:

```bash
herdr plugin install owner/repo[/subdir...]
```

The command works with a public GitHub repository that has a
`herdr-plugin.toml` manifest at its root or in a subdirectory. See
[Plugins](/docs/plugins/) for the manifest and authoring reference.

chunks.anchor: Browse plugins > What a listing shows
chunks.text:
## What a listing shows

Each card shows GitHub repository metadata: the repository name and owner, its
description, star count, primary language, and the time it was last pushed. Its
plugin rows show each manifest's `name` and `version` and link to the exact
source directory. The index records the manifest path, `id`, `name`, `version`,
`platforms`, and `min_herdr_version` together with the exact default-branch
commit. Forks, archived repositories, repositories without a valid plugin
manifest, and malformed manifest metadata are excluded.

---
title: Marketplace
description: Discover community Herdr plugins on GitHub, and get your own plugin listed.
---

The Herdr plugin marketplace indexes community plugins. Browse it at
[herdr.dev/plugins](/plugins/). The index covers public GitHub repositories; it
is not a reviewed catalog.

chunks.anchor: Menus, pages, and stable selection > Account binding
chunks.text:
## Account binding

Hover an agent row or CLI title to inspect usage. `format` picks dashboard gauges or a table. `position` decides where that per-pane popover lives: `hover` and `both` keep it on agent rows and CLI titles; `page` turns the popover off and leaves the accounts page as the only per-pane view (the settings page shows a hint while it is selected). The accounts page is available in every mode. Choices made in Monitor → Settings are saved as client preferences that override `enabled`, `format`, `position`, `hover_delay_ms` and the disabled providers on that machine until "Restore config file values" is used there. Select and bind the account to the pane. A shared vendor name does not identify an account by itself: when an official callback arrives from an unbound pane and that vendor has exactly one configured account, the server binds the pane to it, persists the binding and marks the snapshot as auto-bound; with several accounts for the vendor the callback is rejected with the candidate list and the pane must be bound explicitly. Auto-binding requires `account_usage.enabled` and a callback that carries quota fields.

chunks.anchor: Menus, pages, and stable selection > Account binding
chunks.text:
The per-pane usage popover on agent rows and CLI titles appears after `hover_delay_ms` (400 ms by default) and closes 250 ms after the pointer leaves the row and the popover. It keeps its own scope and never rewrites the accounts page selection; its **Open page** button opens the accounts page. The cross-provider overview lives on the accounts page: its first chip, **All providers**, shows every listed provider at once.

Client preferences are read field by field: an unreadable value (for example an unknown `usage_format`) drops only that field with one diagnostic and keeps the rest. The `usage_*` keys are written back only once they have been set explicitly.

chunks.anchor: Menus, pages, and stable selection > Account binding
chunks.text: The accounts page lists only providers whose official CLI is installed on the connected host — resolved with the same multi-alias PATH and install-layout detection as the integrations settings page (for example codex standalone/nvm/volta/bun), so both surfaces agree. Providers with an explicitly configured account stay listed. `account.usage.providers` reports an `installed` flag per provider; older servers omit the field and keep listing the full registry. Automatic refresh runs on the server while a client shows the data: API accounts every `api_refresh_seconds` (at least 60 s), CLI probes every `cli_refresh_seconds` (at least 300 s; `account.usage.providers` advertises the effective value as `minimum_interval_seconds`), with bounded backoff after failures. Vendors fed by an official callback (Claude Code) or by Herdr's own integration extension (Pi) advertise no polling interval and are refreshed by those pushes. When the accounts page opens without a provider selected it picks the agent running in the focused pane, otherwise the first listed provider. Switching provider or account keeps the previous snapshot dimmed until fresh data arrives; "Switch account" is disabled when the current scope has fewer than two configured accounts, and providers turned off in settings leave the provider chips, the switch candidates and the overview at once. When a codex CLI is found through an install layout, the probe runs it with that layout's bin directory first on `PATH` so npm-shim CLIs resolve their interpreter.

chunks.anchor: Menus, pages, and stable selection > Account binding
chunks.text: On a wide panel (96 columns and up) the detail column also plots how the selected account's tightest quota window moved over time: the client keeps the last 120 samples it saw (polling responses and subscription pushes alike) and draws them as a sparkline under "Usage history". An explicit refresh (`account.usage.refresh`, the account page's refresh action, switching provider or account) is debounced to 10 s per account and still honors vendor backoff (HTTP 429); a debounced response carries `next_allowed_at_ms`. Terminal results (not signed in, unsupported, permission denied) are retried automatically on a slow schedule — 10 min, doubling up to 1 h, at most 6 times — and the hold is lifted as soon as the CLI binary or its credential files change, so signing in heals the account without a restart; an explicit refresh always retries a terminal state. Official callbacks without quota fields do not overwrite the cached sample. After 15 min without a callback the snapshot is shown as cached data; probes may fall back, but only a successful probe or the next callback replaces it. Push-fed vendors (Claude Code's official callback, Pi's extension push) report `callback_only` in the refresh state: an explicit refresh cannot produce a new sample for them, though it may still refresh a login or binding placeholder.

chunks.anchor: Menus, pages, and stable selection > Account binding
chunks.text: While the accounts page is visible, the client subscribes with `account.usage.subscribe` on servers that advertise it and applies pushed `account.usage.updated` / `account.usage.refreshing` events as they arrive, keeping only a 30 s fallback poll; the subscription is dropped when the page is hidden, re-established after a reconnect, and older servers fall back to polling (2 s, or 500 ms while a probe is in flight). An account being probed shows "Refreshing…" on its own row; the refresh button reads "Refresh in N s" while the selected account (or, with no selection, every listed account) is still debounced, and a vendor backoff longer than a minute is noted on the account's row instead of locking the button. The accounts page also carries a binding row: a pane picker that only offers panes running the selected provider's agent, "Bind focused pane", and one-click candidates from `pending_binding` after the server rejected a callback from an unbound pane. Every binding entry refuses a pane running another provider's agent, and enabling the official callback binds the pane on the host that answered — never on a host that became active meanwhile.

chunks.anchor: Menus, pages, and stable selection > Account binding
chunks.text: Claude Code is callback-first. Quota comes from the official statusline callback; probes only check the login state with the non-interactive `claude auth status --json`, which reads the real login store read-only. A signed-in account without the callback shows "waiting for the official statusline callback" together with the setting to enable, and that precheck backs off on the same slow schedule as terminal states until the first callback arrives.
